summary: Defines best practices for creating new top-level media types, the part before the slash in a media type. It introduces a registry for them and gives a short history. It updates RFC 6838.

eli5.summary: File types have family names like text or image. This explains the careful steps for adding a brand new family name.

questions: how to define a new top-level media type
why not use x- prefix for media types
subtitle: The rules for adding a new top-level media type, such as the part before the slash in text/html.

tldr.problem: RFC 6838 gave only summary criteria for creating new top-level media types such as text or image, which are rare and very different from one another.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists required criteria, additional considerations and negative criteria for new top-level types, requires a Standards Track RFC, and creates an IANA registry of top-level types with its initial contents.
tldr.outcome: New top-level types now follow the Standards Action policy and are recorded in the Top-Level Media Types registry; the RFC updates RFC 6838.

today: RFC 9694 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 13) that updates RFC 6838, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. It sets the process for any future top-level type.

sections.title: Top-Level Types and Why They Are Rare
sections.content:
A top-level type is the part to the left of the slash in a media type, as in text/..., application/... or image/.... It is different from a tree (standards, vendor, personal), which sits to the right of the slash. RFC 6838 only briefly gave criteria for more top-level types, so this document gives more detail and updates it.

New top-level types are rare and different enough that each is evaluated separately. The main extension point is the subtype below each type, and the application type can always be used for formats that fit nowhere else.

The top-level type can serve as a fallback when choosing software for a wide range of related formats, and for user-directed information such as default icons. The RFC also warns that a media type may be under an attacker's control.
sections.eli5: A file label has a big family name first, like "image", then a specific name. Brand new family names are rare because the existing ones, plus a catch-all "application", cover nearly everything.

sections.title: Required Criteria
sections.content:
Every new top-level type MUST meet these:

  • It is defined in a Standards Track RFC, which ensures enough community interest, review and consensus.
  • The RFC's IANA Considerations section asks IANA to add the type to the registry of top-level types.
  • The criteria for what does and does not fall under the type are defined clearly. If they cannot be, the thing is probably not suitable as a top-level type.
  • The RFC documents security considerations that apply to all or a significant subset of subtypes.
  • At least one subtype is described. A top-level type with no subtypes serves no purpose.
sections.eli5: To add a new family name you need a proper official document, clear rules about what belongs, a safety note, and at least one real example inside it.

sections.title: Additional and Negative Criteria
sections.content:
Several points count for or against a new type but are not strict rules. Wide existing use of an unregistered top-level type may show a need, yet using unregistered types is highly discouraged. A working group is not required. The defining document should include initial subtype registrations, and several subtypes should be expected, since a single subtype is not enough. Proposers and the user community should commit to emitting and consuming the type. Common parameters, help for humans debugging, shared restrictions (such as CRLF line endings for text) and generic dispatching (such as multipart/* handled as multipart/mixed) are all arguments in favor.

The negative criteria say what is not a reason:

  • A pointer into another registration space that duplicates existing types, such as an oid/nnnnn type.
  • A mapping of other protocol elements such as file extensions or URI schemes. Use one type/subtype with a parameter instead.
  • A general type system for mapping programming languages or ontologies.
  • Aliases for existing widely used types or subtypes (SHOULD NOT).
  • An X- prefix, which cannot be registered and SHOULD NOT be used, in line with RFC 6648.
sections.eli5: Good reasons include many related things sharing the same traits. Bad reasons include just wanting a nickname for something that already has a label.

sections.title: A Short History of Top-Level Types
sections.content:
RFC 1341 first split content types into type and subtype and introduced seven top-level types: text, multipart, message, image, audio, video and application. RFC 1437 defined an extra one, but it was an April Fools RFC and was not registered. RFC 2046 discouraged X- top-level types, and RFC 2048 required a Standards Track RFC for any new one.

Later additions were model (RFC 2077, 1997), example (RFC 4735) and font (RFC 8081, 2017, formalizing widespread unofficial use). RFC 9695 defines haptics and was developed in parallel with this document.

The RFC also notes that chemical is in widespread unofficial use but unregistered, and that local-only uses such as x-scheme-handler and inode/directory on some Linux desktops are not meant for exchange.
sections.eli5: The first seven family names came in one batch. A few more were added later, each through a formal process, while some popular unofficial names never got registered.

sections.title: The Top-Level Media Types Registry
sections.content:
New registrations follow the Standards Action policy. A registration gives the type's name, the defining specification and optional comments, and the specification must contain an IANA Considerations section and document security considerations. There should be at least one subtype, except for demonstration types such as example.

IANA created the "Top-Level Media Types" registry and filled it with eleven types: application, audio, example, font, haptics, image, message, model, multipart, text and video. Each entry holds the name, defining RFC, a pointer to the subtype registry and a comment. The comment for example says no registrations, for examples only, and the one for text says it requires CRLF for newlines.
sections.eli5: There is now an official list of every family name, who defined it, and where to find its members.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document itself is not expected to introduce security issues. The security issues of introducing any new top-level media type MUST be evaluated and documented carefully, which is why the defining RFC must cover them.
sections.eli5: The rulebook is harmless, but anyone adding a new family name must think hard about safety and write it down.
